item.title: Re: Red Herring
item.content:encoded:
Or shortform now I'm not tripping balls at silly oclock in the morning:

Until we were well into 200X, you wouldn't have seriously considered a digital camera for such purposes instead of a decent 35mm SLR. Certainly not for taking pictures you'd then blow up and hang on a wall. The quality just wasn't there, nor the storage capacity, affordability or ruggedness. Sony were still making and successfully selling the floppy-disc-based, XGA-rez Mavica into this century, for heaven's sake. Plus it being a film camera with a self timer would better explain how the face wasn't "seen" until quite recently; 096 simply wasn't looking in the photographer's direction at any time he was looking the other way, including lining up the shot - when it was actually taken, he was instead standing in front of and looking at the camera for a time-delay selfie. The rest of it would just be happy accidents through the development, printing, framing and hanging process, until one day he looked just a little too close and his eyes finally resolved just enough for it to count.

And, as previously said, unless you've inflated a low rez example to the point of obvious blockiness, it's rather hard to make out individual pixels in a printed photo. And if the inlined picture is supposed to be a 1:1 rendition with a 2x2 block of pixels blacked out, you wouldn't want to print that any larger than passport-photo sized; what looks acceptable on a monitor seems hopelessly pixelated when printed at the same scale.

Those two things break the immersion somewhat for me. Everything else in the article is gold, it's just those bits.

+ show block
– hide block

Well, OK, three things - those, and the idea that SCRAMBLE was some kind of system that overlaid an obfuscating layer on an otherwise standard direct-feed nightvision visor, instead of having an all-digital, completely interruptible image path… and modern advancements in AR and face recognition, especially "faceswap" type apps, show it's entirely possible to perform the described processing in realtime with modest hardware; there's occasional gaps with the phone/tablet based flavours, because they prefer showing no-delay live video without the filter, to maintaining the filter with a delay or stuttering, but the foundation version need not conform to that and could have a deliberate 1/30th sec delay where any failure of the processing unit to properly deal with 096's face, or any other visual/memetic threat (which need not be scrambling - simple obscuring would do) would lead to a dropped frame, ie the last successfully rendered one would remain static in place… it'd take some getting used to, and might cause some early-VR style nausea from the necessarily not quite perfect headtracking, but it'd work.

Yes, I know the thing is "supposed to be defective by design", but… (begin even more late night rambling, I'm many hours overdue for food…)

+ show block
– hide block

I just can't see the system as described ever getting past the proposal stage because someone would have put their hand up and said "er, OK, so what if the scrambling chip fails, or doesn't respond fast enough?".

Also, as most NV systems that you have any hope of manipulating the feed through (not counting the very oldskool ones that are pure fluoroscopes/photomultipliers) are essentially either analogue or digital high-sensitivity monochrome video cameras close-coupled to a miniature TV tube or flatpanel, they don't actually necessarily respond instantly; the beam still needs to raster-scan across the scene, taking about a sixtieth of a second (or the CCD and LCD arrays need to be polled and then addressed, in a very similar manner and at about the same speed).

So either you have no delay in the circuit at all - which means no chance of actually blocking out the image, because by the time the computer picks it up it's already passed through the system to the screen (not at the speed of light, but certainly at the speed of electricity), and the next point you can obscure it is 16ms later, by which point the eye has already received a brief but entirely effective subliminal flash (if you don't think that can work, get an old computer and a CRT and program it to show a blank screen, then flick an image on and off it precisely once, for just one frame… you'll still see it fairly clearly)… and in fact if there's any movement at all you're continually running to keep up, with the blanked area trailing behind the actual image even if you use sophisticated motion detection and prediction schemes.

Or you incorporate a delay of some kind (analogue delay line, digital framebuffer… etc), in which case the computer doesn't need to be faster than light (but, come on, tell me, the foundation doesn't have that kind of power anyway?), because it's got plenty of time to process the image and ensure it's safe before ever allowing it to pass to the output stage. Say you incorporate a 20ms delay, which in a 60fps system gives you both 3.3ms in hand between the very end of the received frame and the start of the output, plus whatever actual Vblank period the system natively includes (for NTSC, and closely derived standards like RS343, about an additional 1.25ms)…
…In other words you have almost a clear 5ms to do your facial recognition and very simplistic image censoring (just turn all pixels identified as the target's face black, plus maybe a 4 pixel each side/same pixels on each of 4 lines above and below as a buffer zone) before the image has to start rendering to the screen, which with, say, a 1.5GHz, quad core mobile processor (probably cutting edge when this was written; decidedly old news now) gives you 30 million cycles to play with. If you use some kind of GPU based processing you get far more. And if that's not enough and processing is still ongoing at the point the screen wants to start rendering, just output either the previous frame's contents, or flat black pixels, until you're finally done and can swap in the new buffer. Essentially if the processing load is light, it runs at the full 60fps (or whatever framerate you want) with a fairly minimal lag. If things get a bit heavier, it just suffers a framerate hit and an increase in latency, like online gaming with a low powered computer and slow uplink.

With a suitably powerful system, maybe something mounted in a backpack and utilising desktop or gaming laptop grade GPUs and CPUs, you could get that latency down under the length of a single frame. Maybe even cram it into the Vblank period - as well as operating on the data stream live as it comes into the buffer, without waiting for the buffer to prefill - so the output starts being rendered a little before the camera starts recording the next frame. You'd probably still have to suffer about 15ms all up, or a bit less with a higher framerate, but that certainly seems to be within acceptable bounds for console and most VR gamers…

Now if you'll imagine this second block was nested inside the first, so the third one is actually returning to the first…

+ show block
– hide block

Us armchair wannabe systems engineers on a random webforum are able to pick holes a mile wide in the system, so the foundation's carefully chosen, highly trained and (presumably) well paid, professional programmers and equipment testers should have been able to spot the bugs in the idea and/or the actual hardware before it went anywhere near the field and raise serious red flags about it.

Of course, what's maybe more likely is…
a) they were still in the early testing phases when 096 broke out and someone thought "eh, they're probably better than nothing, they might give us SOME advantage, better than going in with completely unprotected eyes", and everyone got a bit too cocky
b) that, but the field agents were fed a lie about those being the final, ready for primetime, utterly infallible versions. I mean, SCPF, right?
c) the offending doctor found some way to sneak a code bomb into the firmware, so that the goggles tested out just fine, but a week or two after the proposed testing period the filtering routine would be subtly altered to allow just one frame of 096's face to sneak through at the start of a block of censored frames. He'd have to be very good both to get access to the code repository and to keep anyone from discovering the deliberately introduced bug (as well as the odd bit of time dependent code), but hey, he managed to engineer a whole containment breach. Perhaps he's extraordinarily competent. Perhaps he had some kind of special help…

item.title: Re: Red Herring
item.content:encoded:
On top of which, we have the SCRAMBLE system somehow picking up the shyguy lurking in the corner of a photo in the unfortunate -1's house, and not only successfully blurring it out that one time but also ALERTING the MTF leader to its presence so that he was able to do the needle-in-a-haystack job of retrieving it yet not fall foul of the effect himself. From four pixels inside a much larger picture, that the unit's own sensors have to scan and process. It just doesn't gel.

+ show block
– hide block

As well as the rather glaring thing of the photo having been taken some time in the 90s. I was around to witness the early days of digital camera technology towards the end of the decade, and I can tell you something for free - digital cameras, and moreover their storage options and batteries, were shit until we were firmly into the 21st century. No-one would have seriously taken one along to document a hardcore mountaineering trip, and make prints of. Maybe for a few low rez snaps to upload onto a clunky Geocities website when they got home. My mother was able to borrow a fairly fancy Fujifilm model in approx 1998 (unit cost about the same as a decent SLR, and the 2mb and 8mb - meg, not gig - memory cards were each worth the equivalent of quite a few rolls of film and processing), which I co-opted for some school work, and didn't I just feel like the king of technology being able to insert pictures right from the device into an MS Publisher document and then output it on our inkjet printer without having to process and scan them first. However, despite the convenience, the quality was hopeless - it paled not only in comparison to similarly priced film cameras, and the entire range of 35mm's below that, but also the 110 cartridge instamatic that was my own pride and joy. The colour rendition was like a film that had been through a flood and suffered some light leakage before being processed, maximum resolution was just 1280x1024 so borderline for enlarging any bigger than maybe 6x5 inches (or 6x4 with cropping), and even at the maximum quality setting (that gave you maybe 20 shots between the two memory cards) there was noticeable JPEG artefacting.

Other than that brief fling, I didn't bother considering a digital model for my own use until it was pretty much forced by a university project several years later (which involved taking a huge number of pictures for differential analysis, so much so that the film cost alone would have bankrupted me; throwing probably 8x more than I'd ever previously spent on any single camera at a rudimentary 2mpx model - still equal to if not better than the cutting edge in 1998 - and 16mb memory card was a clear moneysaver in comparison), as even the cheapest film formats were still superior, and indeed that first digital model saw service alongside the 110, a 35mm and an APS, as its main advantage was still cost and convenience of quickly turning a lot of low quality shots into illustrations for documents without the celluloid and chemical stages. The state of the art had advanced some by then, but only up to maybe 8mpx and 64mb, and that was up into the realms of plain silly money.

So our mountaineer would have taken a film camera with him, probably a pretty decent SLR (with, of course, a manual optical viewfinder, that he might have got used to not relying on so much if he also had a tripod with a 2D spirit level and FOV guide on it) and a remote shutter release or self-timer in order to take that mountaintop selfie. He wouldn't have seen 096 in a viewfinder or on a screen, or anything like that (and whoever did the processing may have entrusted it to an automated high-volume machine, or - if doing it manually - used tongs that just happened to block out 096's face whilst they were looking at and handling the picture in question)… and it wouldn't have been recorded as any kind of "pixels", but as a riot of variously-exposed film grains.

Maybe the soldier being interviewed was just saying that as a shorthand, or parroting what he was told about the image by someone who was making it up pretty much on the hoof and so got the historical detail wrong… or perhaps the photo in question is a total fake, at best a digital reproduction of an old film original that was processed at what they hoped was a low enough resolution to prevent the effect (may or may not have been successful, we can't tell) or just in a slapdash fashion that pixelated it some, or it could be a complete fabrication, or even one taken rather more recently and be wholly untouched, and they just said it was from "199X".


As a courtesy to our readers on mobile devices, please collapse long posts. ~Zyn

Either way, if that's not a genuine mistake by the author, then it's an additional layer of "this is a big pile of bullshit" that should have been raising red flags even before the twist was revealed.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
As someone in an earlier comment said, the explanation for why the SCRAMBLE gear failed doesn't make sense, but for a slightly different reason: did no-one test the damned things before they were mass-produced? Hand them to a D-Class, and march them into 096's containment chamber. If 096 doesn't react, great. If it does, well, woops. Rinse out the chamber and try again. Putting off such a simple test of potentially life-saving equipment until the moment it's actually needed implies a baffling level of incompetence on the part of Foundation staff.

Further, the idea that 096's escape was engineered by Foundation staff is absurd. 096 went after a random guy who happened to see 4 pixels of its face in a decade-old photo, and tore through every barrier in its way like they were made of paper. What exactly could Dr. Dan have possibly done to make 096's escape any easier, or its rampage any worse? Did he slip that photo to the photographer? Did he sabotage the SCRAMBLE gear? There isn't even any reason for such a stupidly edgy twist - the fact that 096's "rage" state can be triggered by even the smallest, briefest sighting of its face, and therefore has the potential to cause an XK-class scenario at any moment, should be more than enough evidence that the thing is uncontainable and needs to be destroyed.

Speaking of, this thing shouldn't be Euclid. I know it's from a long ways back, before object classes were really set in stone, but this thing seems like a hard Keter to me. It has the potential to kill 99% of the human race, and if it ever gets started, there's nothing the Foundation can do to slow or stop it.
